211.title: Crumbs and Ephphatha (Mark 7:24–37)
211.hook: a foreign mother wins an argument with Jesus, and a deaf man hears be opened
211.howItsDone: In the Catholic rite of baptism for children, the priest may touch the child's ears and mouth and pray that the child soon hear the word and proclaim the faith, a gesture called the Ephphetha, taken from Mark 7.

segments.voice: Yesterday, heart: what makes a person unclean comes out, not in. Your line was out of the heart. Today Jesus walks into foreign land.

Jesus walks north, out of Galilee, into the country around Tyre, on the coast. Foreign land. Mark says he went into a house and wanted nobody to know he was there. It doesn't work. A woman finds him. She isn't Jewish; Mark calls her a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. Her little daughter is tormented by an unclean spirit, and she falls at his feet and begs. What he says back is hard to hear. What she says back to him is quick. Then, on the way home, a man who can't hear.
screen: `NORTH, INTO FOREIGN LAND.` → `A MOTHER AT HIS FEET.` → `A MAN WHO CAN'T HEAR.`

segments.voice: First, the hard line. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Suffer first the children to be filled: for it is not good to take the bread of the children, and cast it to the dogs." Readers take the children as Israel and the dogs as everyone else. It stings. Some hear a test of her faith; some simply let it be hard. Mark doesn't explain. Second, her answer. She doesn't leave. She takes his own picture and turns it: "Yea, Lord; for the whelps also eat under the table of the crumbs of the children." Whelps: young dogs, the ones under the table. Fine, she says, I'm under the table. Crumbs fall. And he gives way: "For this saying go thy way," and her daughter is healed. It's her words, this saying, that he points to. Third, the deaf man. Back near the Sea of Galilee, people bring a man who is deaf and can hardly speak. Jesus takes him aside, away from the crowd, puts his fingers in the man's ears, spits and touches his tongue. He looks up to heaven, groans, and says one word in Aramaic: "Ephpheta, which is, Be thou opened." Mark kept the sound. Fourth, where the word lives now. At a Catholic baptism, the priest may touch the child's ears and mouth and pray that they be opened, to hear the word and proclaim the faith. It's called the Ephphetha rite. A groan by a lake became part of how the Church welcomes a baby.
screen: `THE CHILDREN'S BREAD, AND THE DOGS.` · `EVEN THE WHELPS EAT THE CRUMBS.` · `FINGERS, SPIT, A GROAN, A WORD.` · `THE WORD AT A BAPTISM.` · then, large: `BE THOU OPENED.`

segments.voice: Touch your ears lightly with your fingertips, then your lips, and name one place you've gone closed: a person you stopped listening to, a word you keep swallowing, a door you locked a while ago. If you pray, say the one word Jesus said: be opened. If you don't, let your hands rest open on your knees, and breathe toward that closed place.
Ephphatha. Aramaic: be opened. Spoken to a deaf man by the Sea of Galilee, and still spoken at baptisms. Today's word.
Your line: be opened. The mother made him listen all the way to the end. That's day two hundred eleven.

212.title: Do you not yet understand (Mark 8:1–21)
212.hook: another feeding, and the disciples still worry about bread
212.howItsDone: Many Catholics keep a habit of recalling God's past gifts, often in the evening examen or in thanksgiving after Communion, and preachers often pair Mark's two feedings with the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephphatha: a deaf man's ears, opened with one Aramaic word. Your line was be opened. Today it's the disciples whose ears don't hear.

A crowd of about four thousand has been with Jesus for three days, and they're out of food. The disciples ask where anyone could find bread out here. There are seven loaves and a few small fish. He gives thanks, breaks, and they hand it out. Everyone eats, and seven baskets of scraps are left over. Then they get into a boat, and somebody realizes they've forgotten to bring bread. One loaf. And the worrying starts again, as if they'd never seen it work out.
screen: `FOUR THOUSAND, THREE DAYS, NO FOOD.` → `SEVEN LOAVES, SEVEN BASKETS.` → `ONE LOAF IN THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: First, the second feeding. Mark has told this before: five thousand, five loaves. Now it happens again, with four thousand. Why twice? Many readers notice where it happens: in the Decapolis, the Gentile country Jesus was just walking through. The first crowd was mostly Jewish; this one may not be. Bread for the children, then bread past the edge of the table, right after the mother's crumbs. Second, the leaven. In the boat Jesus warns them: beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod. Mark doesn't say what the leaven is. Luke's Gospel calls it hypocrisy; many readers hear something small that spreads unseen, the way yeast works through dough. And the disciples hear only one word: bread. We forgot the bread. Third, his questions, one after another, in the Douay-Rheims: "Having eyes, see you not? and having ears, hear you not? neither do you remember." Then he makes them count. The five loaves among five thousand: how many baskets left? Twelve, they say. The seven among four thousand? Seven. And he says: "How do you not yet understand?" Mark ends the scene there, with the question hanging. Fourth, the baskets. Mark even uses two different Greek words for them, one for each feeding, as if each basket was its own memory. The disciples aren't stupid. They're simply human: the fear is louder than the memory. Jesus doesn't answer their fear with a new miracle. He asks them to count the old ones.
screen: `A SECOND FEEDING, IN GENTILE COUNTRY.` · `BEWARE THE LEAVEN. WE FORGOT BREAD.` · `TWELVE BASKETS. SEVEN BASKETS.` · `COUNT THE OLD ONES.` · then, large: `HOW DO YOU NOT YET UNDERSTAND?`

segments.voice: Go back to a time you didn't know how it would work out, and it did: money that came through, a friend who showed up, a door that opened when you'd run out of doors. Picture it in detail, where you were and who was there, and count it like a basket; if there's another, count that too. If you pray, simply say thank you for it; if you don't, let the memory sit next to today's worry.
Leaven. The small hidden thing Jesus warns about in the boat, of the Pharisees and of Herod, that spreads unseen through dough. Today's word.
Your line: remember the baskets. Fear talks loud, and the baskets are still there to count. Day two hundred twelve, done.

213.title: Men as trees, walking (Mark 8:22–26)
213.hook: the only healing done in two stages
213.tomorrow: who do you say I am
213.howItsDone: The Catechism speaks of conversion as an ongoing task rather than a single moment, and Catholics return to confession and prayer again and again; the anointing of the sick can be received more than once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaven, seven baskets and one loaf in a boat. Your line was remember the baskets. Jesus asked, having eyes, see you not? Today, a man who can't see at all.

A broken arm, a broken heart, a bad year: some things get better slowly. There's a day when it's not fixed, but not what it was either. Blurry. In between. Up to now in Mark, a word or a touch has been enough. Today it takes two. The boat lands at Bethsaida, a town on the lake, and people bring Jesus a blind man and beg him to touch him.
screen: `GETTING BETTER SLOWLY.` → `A BLIND MAN AT BETHSAIDA.` → `A HEALING IN TWO STEPS.`

segments.voice: First, the walk. Jesus takes the blind man by the hand and leads him out of the village: a guide walking slowly, watching the ground for both of them. He heals him away from the crowd, like the deaf man two days ago. Second, the first try. He spits on the man's eyes, lays his hands on him, and asks if he sees anything. The man looks up. In the Douay-Rheims: "I see men as it were trees, walking." Shapes. Tall blurs moving. Better than dark, and not right yet. Third, the second touch. Jesus lays his hands on his eyes again, and now the man sees all things clearly. Why two stages? The Gospel doesn't say, so readers look at where Mark put the story. Just before it, the disciples in the boat: eyes that don't see. Just after it, tomorrow's scene, where Peter gets the answer right and the meaning wrong. Some readers hear this healing as a picture of the disciples themselves: they see something, men as trees, and they'll need a second touch. Fourth, the quiet mercy of it. The man is honest. He doesn't pretend to see clearly to be polite; he says: blurry. And Jesus doesn't scold him. He just touches him again. The Catechism speaks of conversion in a similar way, as an ongoing task, not a single moment: the second touch, and the third.
screen: `LED BY THE HAND OUT OF TOWN.` · `THE FIRST TOUCH: BLURRY SHAPES.` · `THE SECOND TOUCH: EVERYTHING CLEAR.` · `A PICTURE OF THE DISCIPLES.` · then, large: `I SEE MEN AS IT WERE TREES, WALKING.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing in you that's healing slowly, a grief, a habit, a body, a friendship, and without grading it, say honestly where it is, the way the man did: it's blurry, it's better than before, it isn't done. Rest your hands over your eyes for a few breaths. If you pray, ask for the second touch; if you don't, let it be halfway for now, without hurrying it.
Second touch. The touch that made the blurry shapes a blind man saw at Bethsaida go clear: healing that came in two stages. Today's word.
Your line: healing in stages. Blurry is a stage, not a failure. See you tomorrow.

214.title: Who do you say I am (Mark 8:27–38)
214.hook: Peter gets the answer right and the meaning wrong
214.howItsDone: Catholics profess who Jesus is each Sunday in the Creed, and Catholic devotion speaks of daily hardships as crosses carried with Christ, sometimes offering them up in prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, second touch: blurry first, then clear. Your line was healing in stages. Today, Peter sees half of it.

What are people saying about me? From a friend, it's usually a nervous question. Today Jesus asks it, and he doesn't sound nervous. He's walking with his disciples on the road to the villages of Caesarea Philippi, in the north, and he asks: who do people say I am? The answers come fast. John the Baptist, back from the dead. Elijah. One of the prophets. Then he turns the question around, and there's nowhere to hide from it.
screen: `WHAT DO PEOPLE SAY ABOUT ME?` → `ON THE ROAD TO CAESAREA PHILIPPI.` → `JOHN, ELIJAH, A PROPHET.`

segments.voice: First, the right answer. In the Douay-Rheims: "But whom do you say that I am? Peter answering said to him: Thou art the Christ." Christ isn't a last name. It's a title, the Greek for anointed, and John's Gospel matches it to the Hebrew: "the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ." Israel's kings were anointed with oil. Some readers call this the hinge of Mark's Gospel: near the middle, a disciple finally says it out loud. Second, the wrong meaning. Right away Jesus starts teaching, openly, Mark says, that the Son of man must suffer many things, be rejected, be killed, and rise again after three days. Peter takes him aside and rebukes him. In Peter's picture, it seems, the Christ doesn't die. Third, the rebuke back, and it's sharp: "Go behind me, Satan, because thou savourest not the things that are of God, but that are of men." Some readers dwell on the opening words. Go behind me: where a disciple walks. Peter has stepped in front, trying to lead, and Jesus sends him back to his place. Fourth, the invitation to everyone. Jesus calls the crowd over too: "If any man will follow me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." In Rome's world a cross wasn't jewelry. It was an execution, carried out in public, and Mark's own story will end at one. Catholics read it as the shape of the whole Christian life: not a grim road, but following someone who walked it first.
screen: `THOU ART THE CHRIST.` · `THE SON OF MAN MUST SUFFER.` · `GO BEHIND ME: A DISCIPLE'S PLACE.` · `TAKE UP YOUR CROSS AND FOLLOW.` · then, large: `WHOM DO YOU SAY THAT I AM?`

segments.voice: Imagine the road, the dust, and the question turned toward you: not what the Church says, not what your parents said, but who do you say he is? Maybe the answer is sure, maybe it's I don't know yet, maybe it's a question back; any honest sentence counts, so say it quietly, once, and sit with it. If you pray, you can offer that sentence as your prayer.
Christ. Not a last name but a title, Greek for anointed: what Peter calls Jesus at Caesarea Philippi, and the hinge of Mark's Gospel. Today's word.
Your line: take up your cross. Peter had the name right; the road was the hard part. Two hundred fourteen days in.

215.title: The mountain again (Mark 9:1–13)
215.hook: the transfiguration, then down the mountain into need
215.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Feast of the Transfiguration on August 6, and the story is read every year on the Second Sunday of Lent, as a glimpse of glory before the road to the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ: Peter got the answer right and the meaning wrong. Your line was take up your cross. Six days later, a mountain.

Some moments you want to bottle. A wedding night. A retreat. A concert where everyone sang the last chorus together. Going home feels wrong. Today three fishermen get a moment like that, and a far stranger one. Six days after the hard talk about the cross, Jesus leads Peter, James and John up a high mountain, alone. In Mark, mountains are where things happen: he went up one to pray, and up one to call the twelve. This time something happens to him. And then they have to walk back down.
screen: `MOMENTS YOU WANT TO BOTTLE.` → `THREE FRIENDS, A HIGH MOUNTAIN.` → `THEN, THE WALK BACK DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the change. Mark says he was transfigured before them, his clothes shining white, whiter than any cloth-bleacher on earth could make them. A detail about laundry, right next to the glory of God. Second, the company. Elijah and Moses appear, talking with Jesus. Tradition hears the Law in Moses and the prophets in Elijah: the story of Israel, on one mountaintop with him. Third, Peter. He blurts out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Rabbi, it is good for us to be here: and let us make three tabernacles." Tents. Stay. Keep it. Mark adds, kindly, that Peter didn't know what to say; they were terrified. Then a cloud covers them, and a voice: "This is my most beloved son; hear ye him." Not build him a tent. Listen. Suddenly, looking around, they see no one but Jesus only. Fourth, the way down. On the path he tells them to tell no one until the Son of man has risen from the dead, and they argue about what rising from the dead could even mean. They ask about Elijah, and he says Elijah has already come. Mark doesn't name him; in Matthew's telling, the disciples understand he means John the Baptist. Mark lets no one stay on the mountain. At the bottom, tomorrow, a crowd and a desperate father are already waiting.
screen: `TRANSFIGURED: WHITER THAN BLEACH.` · `MOSES AND ELIJAH WITH HIM.` · `LET US BUILD THREE TENTS.` · `THE WALK DOWN, AND ELIJAH.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY MOST BELOVED SON; HEAR YE HIM.`

segments.voice: Sit for a minute and rest: if you pray, in whatever prayer you have, or in the words hear ye him; if you don't, in the quiet, like a view from a high place. Then walk down the mountain in your mind and see who's at the bottom today, someone who needs a call, a ride, a meal, an apology. Pick one person, and the one thing you'll do.
Transfigured. What happened to Jesus before Peter, James and John on the mountain: his clothes shining white, Moses and Elijah beside him, and a voice saying hear him. Today's word.
Your line: down the mountain. The voice said listen, not stay. Day two hundred fifteen, done.

216.title: Help my unbelief (Mark 9:14–29)
216.hook: a father cries I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief
216.howItsDone: Catholics use the father's words from Mark 9 as a short prayer in times of doubt, and the Catechism describes faith as seeking understanding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, transfigured: Jesus shining, a voice saying hear him, then the walk back down. Your line was down the mountain. Today, who was waiting at the bottom.

A hospital hallway, someone you love behind the door, and no news: that's where this father has been living. Jesus comes down the mountain into an argument: a crowd, some scribes, and the other disciples, who've failed. A man brought his son to them. Since childhood the boy has had fits: a spirit throws him down, he foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth, goes rigid. It has thrown him into fire and into water. The disciples couldn't help. Now the father turns to Jesus, too tired to be polite.
screen: `A HOSPITAL HALLWAY.` → `THE DISCIPLES COULDN'T HELP.` → `A FATHER TOO TIRED TO BE POLITE.`

segments.voice: First, the request: if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us. If you can. Some readers hear years of disappointment in those three words. Second, Jesus throws it back. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth." The question isn't whether Jesus can. It's whether the father can believe. Third, the cry. Mark says the father cried out at once, with tears: "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." I believe. I don't believe enough. Both true at once. And Jesus doesn't wait for a purer faith. He heals the boy with the faith this man actually has, half of it doubt. The boy goes still as a corpse, and people say he's dead. Jesus takes him by the hand and lifts him, and he stands up. Fourth, afterward, indoors, the disciples ask why they couldn't do it. In the Douay: "This kind can go out by nothing, but by prayer and fasting." The failure, as Jesus names it, wasn't technique. This needed prayer. And the father's cry has stayed in Catholic prayer: short enough to say in a hallway, honest enough for the nights when faith is thin.
screen: `IF YOU CAN DO ANYTHING.` · `ALL THINGS ARE POSSIBLE TO HIM THAT BELIEVETH.` · `HE HEALS WITH THE FAITH THERE IS.` · `THIS KIND NEEDS PRAYER.` · then, large: `I DO BELIEVE, LORD: HELP MY UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: Notice how much you believe today, about God, about yourself, about anything that matters to you, without inflating it or shrinking it. If you pray, say the father's words slowly on your breath: I do believe, Lord, breathing in; help my unbelief, breathing out. If you don't, simply let both be true at once, the part of you that trusts and the part that doesn't.
Unbelief. What a desperate father confessed to Jesus in the same breath as his faith: I do believe, Lord, help my unbelief. Today's word.
Your line: bring your doubt along. The father brought his, and Jesus didn't send him away. See you tomorrow.

217.title: A child in the middle (Mark 9:30–50)
217.hook: they argue who's greatest; he puts a child among them
217.howItsDone: In the Catholic Church the diaconate takes its name from this servant word, and the Pope's traditional title, Servant of the Servants of God, echoes the same teaching about being last of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, unbelief: a father cried out with faith and doubt in one breath, and Jesus answered. Your line was bring your doubt along. Today ends the week.

The drive home when the kids in the back seat have been fighting, and the second you ask what's going on, it goes silent. That's today. Walking through Galilee, Jesus tells his disciples a second time that he'll be handed over and killed and rise again. Mark says they didn't understand, and they were afraid to ask. So they talked about something else, just out of his hearing. Home in Capernaum, he asks what they were arguing about on the road. Nobody says a word.
screen: `SILENCE IN THE BACK SEAT.` → `HE'LL BE KILLED. THEY'RE AFRAID TO ASK.` → `WHAT WERE YOU ARGUING ABOUT?`

segments.voice: First, the argument: which of them was the greatest. Right after he told them he was going to die. It's almost funny, and very human. Second, he sits down. In that world a teacher sat to teach, so Mark is saying: this is the lesson. He calls the twelve and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any man desire to be first, he shall be the last of all, and the minister of all." The Greek for minister is diakonos, a servant, the one who waits on tables. It's where the Church gets the word deacon. Third, the child. He stands a little child in the middle of them, then wraps his arms around the child. In his world a child had no status: no rights, no say, nobody's idea of great. And he says: "Whosoever shall receive one such child as this in my name, receiveth me." Welcome the one who can't do anything for you, and you've welcomed him. Fourth, the rest of the chapter turns the same idea. John complains that a stranger is driving out demons in Jesus's name, and Jesus says let him be: "he that is not against you, is for you." Even a cup of water given in his name won't lose its reward. The chapter ends: have peace among you. Look back at this week in Mark: crumbs under the table, the baskets, men as trees, who do you say I am, the mountain, a father's cry. And now a child in the middle, where the greatest one should be.
